extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, classics, literary criticism, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Critical commentary on Book III–IV of Plato's Republic highlighting pedagogical, ethical, stylistic, and artistic standards implicit in Plato's text and the commentator's evaluation of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's moral influence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a music of the soul which answers to the harmony of the world; good music will give harmony to the soul and so greatly diminish the need of medicine and law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music should be simple and characteristic; it acts through habit in early education to form natural good taste and a feeling of truth and beauty. Dangerous or corrupt melodies (compared to Lydian and Ionian melodies) must be forbidden because musical change can secretly alter characters, social relations, and institutions. Good music is part of the 'true Greek atmosphere' for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic and bodily training for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is related to the body as cause to effect; therefore guardians require a simpler kind of gymnastic, akin to their simple music, and must be inured to changes of food and climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians must abstain from strong drink; ordinary gymnastic may be sleepy and harmful if stopped suddenly; warrior-athletes need to be 'wide-awake' and hardy. Dietal rules (Homeric model) favour roast meat only, no fish or boiled meats, and reject sweet sauces and decadent cookery (Sicilian, Attic confections). Excessive gluttony and intemperance corrupt a state and create dependency on law and medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal living and poverty for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should have no private property; their pay should only meet expenses; they should have common meals and must not touch gold and silver or live under the same roof with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private houses, lands, or money make guardians into householders and tradesmen, turning them into enemies and tyrants. The 'divine gift' of gold in their souls must not be alloyed. This rule prevents luxury, avarice and the degeneration of guardians into boon companions or tyrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and testing of rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers must be the elders who love their subjects most and think they have a common interest with them; they must be watched at every epoch of life to ensure they retain principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must be 'tried by many tests, like gold in the refiner’s fire'—passed through danger, pleasure, grief, and pain—emerging victorious and unstained, with all faculties harmoniously exercised. Younger men may be called 'auxiliaries'; the select elders receive highest honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate professional experience: physician vs judge
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician should have had experience of disease in his own body because he cures with his mind; the judge should not have his mind corrupted by crime and therefore should be of a certain age and have been innocent in youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judge gains insight into vice by observing others rather than practicing it; a criminal-turned-detective is overly suspicious and errs among good men. The ideal judge combines late-acquired insight with early innocence. This distinction shapes eligibility and evaluation of these professions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must conform to subject and metre to style
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The style is to conform to the subject and the metre to the style.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought should not exceed the power of lucid expression; there must be proportion between style and subject. Poets whose language is obscure or whose sequence is tangled fail this rule. The critic should demand harmony between idea and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, beauty, and ease in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no poetry without beauty, or beauty without ease and clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure passages where thought outruns expression: half-expressed figures, harsh constructions, distorted collocations, and remote sequences of ideas. The poet is often a bad judge of his own meaning; therefore poetry ought to aim for clear language and proportion. Modern poets have no excuse for reverting to earlier obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: True art as simple, ideal, and moral
rubrics_metrics.description: True art is not fanciful and imitative, but simple and ideal—the expression of the highest moral energy, whether in action or repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art of noble simplicity (plastic art, characteristic strains of music) best influences youth and forms natural good taste. This conception of art pervades nature and is an aspect of reason, used in preliminary education and habit-formation, not limited to plastic arts or music alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and literature judged as a coherent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art, like the State, is a whole; harmony, symmetry, measure, proportion, and unity are the principles of criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgement should seek unity and proportion in artworks; the notion of a 'whole' underlies both politics and art, and is the key standard for assessing excellence in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myth (the 'noble lie') as pedagogical device
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnificent lie (the tale of earthborn men and metals in the soul) is to be imparted first to rulers, then soldiers, lastly to the people to secure social cohesion and duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The myth teaches that people are born of earth and fashioned with gold, silver, brass, or iron natures; while this is a fiction, its gravity and analogy to Greek tradition make it a useful educational instrument. It also allows for transposition of ranks by merit (a golden parent may have a silver son), and is presented as a 'monstrous fiction' to overcome resistance to novel principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of ranks and merit over caste
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a distinction of ranks dependent on circumstances but this distinction ought to be broken through from time to time in favour of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato proposes tests by which those who fall short are removed or not admitted to governance; periodic breaking of caste (transposition of ranks) is necessary to avoid rigid social order. The idea is presented mythologically to soften resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of education and resistance to cultural innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the great matter; the guardians should preserve music and gymnastic from innovation because altering a country's songs will alter its laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If education remains established, a restorative process will correct deficiencies and supply self-government. Minute enactments are unnecessary in good states and useless in bad ones; education should be entrusted to guardians who will in turn manage other affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between music and gymnastic to harmonize soul's principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic correspond to reason and passion respectively; mingling them in harmonious concord produces the true guardian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive gymnastic hardens and brutalizes; too much music enervates and melts away spiritedness. Too little spirit exhausts; too much causes irritability. The training must strike a balance so the body serves as ally or instrument to the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public approach to medicine consistent with civic welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians in a well-ordered State should not preserve useless lives; medicine should serve the public interest rather than pampering the rich or creating a culture of nursing diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censure of a medical system that nurses chronic invalidism (Herodicus) and praise for Asclepius' 'kill or cure' artisan practice. The State's limited leisure means citizens should not be indulged into ill-health; remedies should be appropriate and not preserve intemperate or worthless subjects even for profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of the State: duty before happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution is designed for the good of the whole, not primarily to make individual citizens happy; first duty, then happiness is the natural moral order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilitarian considerations are a valuable corrective and often coincide with right, but are not the historical basis of morality. The State must prioritize right and truth (duty) over mere pleasure or comfort; happiness may follow in a well-ordered State but is secondary to duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic devices characteristic of Plato's presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato often uses rhetorical and stylistic arts—affected ignorance of music, tentative construction of the State, alternating description of the State as reality and imagination, connecting links toward the expulsion of poets, and satirical companion pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices sustain reader interest and serve argumentative ends; they are features to recognize and evaluate when assessing Plato's style and method rather than mistakes to be corrected.
